After a stock-market crash, a balanced mix needs a rule: compare rebalancing with drift

Follow a 60/40 portfolio through a crash, a recovery and a second decline. See how the equity share drifts, what rebalancing trades buy and sell, and when the rule helps or hurts.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 26 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 26 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Both portfolios start with the same money and target. Annual asset returns are authored inputs, applied to each bucket for the full year. The rebalanced portfolio trades back to the target at a year-end only when equity is off target by more than the entered band. The central idea

A crash lowers the equity share of a balanced portfolio. Rebalancing buys equity after the fall to restore the risk level you chose; it helped in the authored recovery and added to losses when a second decline followed. Inside a balanced fund the manager does this for you, while in a self-managed non-registered account the trades can have tax consequences.

01

A crash changes the mix before it changes your plan

A balanced portfolio holds equities and bonds in a chosen proportion. When equities fall much more than bonds, the equity share shrinks even though nobody traded. In the default scenario, a CAD 100,000 portfolio at 60% equity loses 35% on equity and gains 2% on bonds in year one. It ends the year at CAD 79,800, with only 48.9% in equity.

FINRA describes rebalancing as adjusting periodically to stay near a target allocation, by redirecting new money, adding to lagging assets or selling part of outperforming holdings. It also says there is no official timeline for when to rebalance and suggests considering it as part of an annual review. The first chart shows both portfolios’ equity share after any year-end trade.

02

Rebalancing after a crash means buying what just fell

The rebalanced portfolio trades back to 60% when equity is more than five percentage points off target at a year-end. After the crash, it sells about CAD 8,880 of bonds and buys equity. That is uncomfortable by design: the rule follows the allocation, not the headlines.

The trade chart shows each year-end purchase or sale. During the recovery the equity share rises again, so later trades sell equity. Over the default ten years, the rebalanced portfolio buys about CAD 8,880 of equity and sells about CAD 11,834.

Inside a balanced mutual fund or asset-allocation fund, the portfolio manager rebalances within the fund according to its mandate. You do not place those trades, but they can still affect the fund’s taxable distributions in a non-registered account. In a self-managed non-registered account, CRA’s capital gains guide explains that disposing of capital property such as fund units or shares can produce a capital gain or loss. Within a TFSA, income earned is generally tax-free, and in an RRSP tax is generally deferred until withdrawal. The account’s tax rules belong to the wrapper, not the fund.

03

Recovery helps the rebalanced mix; a second decline hurts it first

The value chart follows both portfolios. With three 15% equity recovery years and 6% afterwards, the default rebalanced portfolio ends at about CAD 142,505, versus CAD 137,373 for the drifting portfolio. It held more equity when equities recovered.

The variant chart changes the order of returns. If year two brings a second, smaller decline of 17.5% before the recovery, the rebalanced portfolio has already bought equity and its year-end value falls to about CAD 72,379, versus CAD 74,199 for the drifting mix. It still ends ahead in that variant only because a recovery is assumed afterwards. With no crash, the drifting portfolio’s equity share rises to about 67% and it ends slightly higher, CAD 161,208 versus CAD 160,715, while carrying more equity risk than its target.

No rule guarantees a better outcome. Rebalancing is mainly a way to keep the portfolio’s risk close to the level you chose, rather than letting recent returns choose it.

04

Choose the band, the calendar and the cash source in advance

Set the band to zero to rebalance at every year-end. A wider band trades less often and lets the mix move further before acting. Every trade can involve costs, spreads, sales charges or tax in a non-registered account; this model deducts none of them, so its results flatter frequent trading.

New contributions can do some of the work without sales. Directing a regular deposit to the underweight asset can close part of the gap, as shown in the buy-only rebalancing guide. If you are withdrawing money, choosing which asset to sell can also move the mix; see withdrawal sale sources.

05

A plan for crash worry that does not depend on predicting the crash

  1. Choose a target mix you could hold through a large equity decline, given your horizon, income and other cash.
  2. Keep near-term spending money outside the long-term portfolio.
  3. Write the rebalancing rule: calendar date, band and whether new contributions are used first.
  4. For a fund, read the Fund Facts and prospectus for its target mix, rebalancing approach, fees and risk rating.
  5. For a self-managed account, check the tax effect of each sale outside registered plans before trading.
  6. Review the mix after a major life change, not after each market headline.

The balanced-fund stress guide adds inflation and fees to a crash scenario, and the loss-recovery guide separates recovering a dollar balance from recovering purchasing power.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 26 October 2026. All annual returns, rebalancing bands and portfolio values are hypothetical editable inputs. They are not historical crisis returns, forecasts, probabilities or a promised recovery date. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. FINRA · Asset Allocation and Diversification ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026 for rebalancing methods, the absence of an official rebalancing timeline, annual review, fees and potential tax on sales in taxable accounts. US tax rules are not applied.

  2. CRA · Capital Gains – 2025 (T4037) ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026 for capital property such as mutual fund units and shares, and dispositions that can produce a capital gain or loss. No personal tax amount is calculated.

  3. CRA · What is a TFSA ↗

    Page dated 17 September 2026; reviewed 26 October 2026 for the general tax treatment of income earned in a TFSA.

  4. CRA · Registered Retirement Savings Plan ↗

    Reviewed 26 October 2026 for income sheltered within the plan and generally taxable payments out of it. No personal tax-rate comparison is modeled.

  5. FINRA · What Is Market Timing? ↗

    Published 10 June 2025; reviewed 26 October 2026 for the risk of missing rebounds after selling during a decline. The return paths here are hypothetical.
